# 1 Timothy 3: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I could and couldn't find:** I ran out of searches, so some verses (3, 5, 9, 12, 14) have thinner notes. I found nothing from Lutheran sites, Orthodox sites (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or newadvent.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those areas are left out. The NET Bible and Calvin pages were read in full, so they appear as plain URLs without citation tags.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Paul has just ruled out women holding doctrinal authority over congregations (ch. 2), but he did not want to leave the impression that just *any* man is qualified. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- "Good work" means two things for Guzik. The office is noble, so Timothy must look for noble men. And leadership isn't all about titles and honor and glory; it's about **work**. He cites Spurgeon against lazy ministers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) says that whatever people now think of the office as a career step, then it was thought a good work. He says the desire for it should aim at God's glory and the good of souls. He links this to the Church of England ordination question about being moved by the Holy Spirit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_003.cfm
- The NET Bible note links "trustworthy saying" to 1 Tim 1:15, 4:9, 2 Tim 2:11 and Titus 3:8. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3

**v. 2**
- **Above reproach.** Guzik says the word literally means "Nothing to take hold upon." It is shown by a track record over time, not by being perfect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- The Pulpit Commentary says the word means "not open to attack," a picture possibly taken from wrestling. https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- **"Husband of one wife": the main debate.** The Pulpit Commentary lists three possible senses: that a bishop must have a wife (and so the Russian Church understands it), a ban on polygamy, or a ban on second marriage. It says the Anglicans Wordsworth, Ellicott and Alford all held the third view. https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican) says the early writers, church councils and the Greek Church read the verse as a bar on second marriages for presbyters and deacons. https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- Benson (Methodist) disagrees. The phrase does not mean a bishop must marry, nor that he cannot remarry. He takes it to mean one wife at a time, against widespread polygamy and unjust divorce. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary (JFB) takes the phrase as confuting the celibacy of Rome's priesthood, yet also reads it as "married only once." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- Gill (Baptist) rejects a symbolic reading ("husband of one church"), because the passage goes on to talk about his house and children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- Meyer reads the phrase as a ban on sexual immorality, especially keeping a concubine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- Sam Storms (charismatic) surveys six views. He rejects the Catholic "wife = the Church" reading as invented to enforce priestly celibacy. He also rejects the "never divorced" view. He holds that the man must be a faithful "one-woman man." https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/1-timothy-3:2-12
- Guzik agrees: the phrase describes faithful devotion, not a requirement to be married. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- GotQuestions prefers "one-woman man" too. It adds that an unbiblical divorce may disqualify a man under "above reproach" rather than under this phrase. https://www.gotquestions.org/husband-one-wife.html
- The NET note lists the readings that exclude unmarried, polygamous, divorced, or remarried-widower men, against the NEB's "faithful to his one wife." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
- T. Croskery (Pulpit Commentary homiletics) says the verse condemns Rome's celibacy rule. He also faults the Greek Church, which does not force pastors to marry yet keeps bishoprics for unmarried monks. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_timothy/3-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik takes "covetous" more broadly than love of money. The covetous man is never satisfied with anything, always demanding something more or different. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/

**v. 4**
- Guzik says a leader proves himself first at home. When a child rebels, the question is whether it happened *because* of the parents or *in spite* of their job as parents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- The NET note says "with all dignity" may describe the children rather than the father, as in "children who are obedient and respectful." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
- Matthew Henry says the best way to keep those under you in order is to be grave with them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_003.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: a man who cannot run his household well has no business trying to care for God's church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: "novice" literally means "newly planted." New believers need time to put down roots. He quotes Calvin on how puffed up novices can be, and says promoting them too fast invites the devil's own sin, pride. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- The NET note says the "condemnation of the devil" could mean the judgment the devil himself received, or a punishment the devil brings. It points to 1 Tim 1:20. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3

**v. 7**
- The Biblical Illustrator says Christ's representatives cannot afford... to defy the world's opinion about us so far as moral reputation is concerned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-timothy-3.html
- The NET note says the parallel in 2 Tim 2:26 supports reading "the devil's trap" (a trap the devil sets). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3

**v. 8**
- Guzik says deacon qualifications largely match the overseer's, and neither office is more prestigious: Each is more a matter of *calling* than status. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- Matthew Henry says deacons looked after the church's practical matters (supporting ministers, caring for the poor; Acts 6). Greed would be especially dangerous because they handled church money and might be tempted to embezzle it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_003.cfm
- The NET Bible translates "double-tongued" as "two-faced," with "insincere" or "deceitful" as alternatives. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3

**v. 9**
- The NET note: "the mystery of the faith" means the revealed truths of Christianity. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
- Bible.org: teaching is not the deacon's main role, but they must know God's Word and practice it faithfully. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-deacons

**v. 10**
- Guzik: fitness is shown by conduct, so deacons and bishops are more *recognized* than *appointed*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- William Kelly notes that although deacons dealt with outward things, they still had to be tested first. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html

**v. 11: deacons' wives or women deacons? (a real dividing line)**
- **Women deacons.**
  - Ellicott says Chrysostom and most ancient commentators saw these women as deaconesses. He names Phoebe (Rom 16:1) as an example. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-11.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary homiletics also says the verse refers to deaconesses, asking why deacons' wives would get rules when ministers' wives don't. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_timothy/3-11.htm
  - Bible.org (one study) argues for female deacons. There is no "their" in the Greek, and the deacon role is not a teaching or ruling post, so it would not break 2:12. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-qualities-deacons-and-deaconesses-faithful-servants-1-timothy-38-13
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) allows either reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html
- **Deacons' wives.**
  - Barnes argues this is the natural reading, and that the Greek word alone never means deaconesses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-11.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) prefers deacons' wives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-11.htm
  - Calvin (Reformed) thinks it means the wives of both deacons and bishops, for they must be aids to their husbands in their office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ) strongly rejects "female deacons." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html
  - The NET note tentatively prefers "wives." Its reasons: it would be odd to discuss women deacons in the middle of the men's list, and v. 12 says deacons are "husbands of one wife." It admits the decision is hard. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
- **Methodist voices.**
  - Clarke reads the verse as Christian women in general. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html
  - Benson takes it as deacons' wives, though possibly women in general and women holding church office. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-11.htm
  - Wesley's 1755 New Testament translates it "their wives." https://studylight.org/bible/nas/1-timothy/3-11.html
- **Scholarly summary.** Constable says most interpreters through history preferred the deaconess view, others hold the wives view, and exegetically it is very hard to decide. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html
- **"Not slanderers."** Guzik, citing Clarke: the Greek literally means "not devils." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/

**v. 12**
- The NET note gives the same alternative readings as for v. 2 ("married only once," "devoted solely to their wives"). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
- William Kelly: overseers and deacons alike must run their children and households well. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-11.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: God remembers faithful service even in humble tasks, and he expects to see more **deacons** with a great reward than bishops or pastors. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- The NET notes link this verse to Jesus' teaching that the great must be servants (diakonos). They say "the faith" here means Christian truth, and "confidence" probably means the deacon's own boldness to act on his convictions. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3

**v. 14**
- Calvin: Paul's hope of coming was meant to encourage Timothy and to check those who grew bolder while Paul was away. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/iii.v.iii.htm
- Guzik's quoted source says Timothy's post was temporary, as Paul's representative at Ephesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/

**v. 15: "pillar and foundation of the truth" (Protestant–Catholic divide)**
- **Protestant readings.**
  - Ellicott: the Church is pictured as a massive pillar, holding up and displaying before men and angels the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-15.html
  - Calvin: the Church is the pillar because it defends and spreads the truth through preaching. He rejects the claim that this makes Rome unable to err, and turns the verse around: where truth is buried, there is no true church. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/iii.v.iii.htm
  - Matthew Henry: Scripture's authority does not rest on the Church. The Church holds up the Scripture the way a pillar holds up a posted notice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_003.cfm
  - Gill (Baptist) leans toward applying the phrase to Timothy himself. He adds that when a church stops being the pillar of truth, believers ought to leave it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-15.html
  - Spurgeon (Baptist): the Church does not create truth, and a church that is unfaithful to the truth is "unchurched." https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_timothy/3-15.htm
  - JFB: the phrase describes the Church, not (as some sixteenth-century readers held) the "mystery" in v. 16. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-15.html
  - Bible.org: truth is the foundation of the church's life, but here the church serves the truth as its mission. It notes the many pillars of the Temple of Diana at Ephesus. https://bible.org/seriespage/9-god-s-mission-church-1-timothy-314-16
- **Catholic readings.**
  - Haydock's Catholic commentary ties the verse to Christ's promise to guide his Church by the Spirit of truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/3-15.html
  - Catholic Answers applies the title directly to the Catholic Church, which it says teaches with Jesus' authority. https://www.catholic.com/tract/pillar-of-fire-pillar-of-truth
- **Evangelical response.** GotQuestions argues the verse cannot support an inerrant magisterium. The church holds up the truth but is not its source. https://www.gotquestions.org/church-pillar-foundation-truth.html

**v. 16**
- **Textual note (modern scholarship).**
  - The NET Bible argues the original reading is "He who" (Greek *hos*) rather than "God" (*theos*). Its reasons: the early Alexandrian and Western manuscripts and versions support it; no early patristic writer cites "God"; and the two words looked alike in manuscripts. It treats the verse as a six-line hymn, which explains why there is no antecedent. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
  - The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) translation reads "which was manifested." https://biblehub.com/catholic/1_timothy/3-15.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** He followed the Greek copies he had, which read "God." He saw the line as teaching two natures in one person, against Arius, Nestorius and Eutyches. "Justified in the Spirit" means Christ was shown to be the Son of God despite the weakness of his flesh. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/iii.v.iii.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** The mystery is Christ himself, set out in six statements, and the first proves his deity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_003.cfm
- **Guzik.** He calls it an early hymn, and says that beholding Jesus is what truly transforms our character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- **Barclay.** One possible meaning of "vindicated by the Spirit" is that the Spirit kept Jesus sinless throughout his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/1-timothy-3.html
- **Biblical Illustrator.** The fact of the incarnation is declared, but how it happened is kept hidden. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-timothy-3.html

---

**Church government (affects the whole chapter)**
- Guzik says the passage gives no guidance on structure or on how the offices relate to each other. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-3/
- JFB says Timothy exercised at Ephesus the power that bishops (in the later sense) exercised afterward. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/3-2.htm
- The NET note on v. 2 argues against a single top leader. "The overseer" refers to the class of overseers, as Paul's switches between singular and plural show. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ti&chapter=3
